## Setting
Setting the cleaning arrangement for the shared areas. Five housemates share a kitchen, a bathroom, and a living room, and the informal habit they started with has stopped working. They are settling on one arrangement for the coming year. Participants: Rin, Ryuji, Daisuke, Mio and Victoria. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Bathroom spray stock and the tin's receipts
- Management office rate sheet and billing
- Stopwatch timing of a full pass
- Standard terms of the outside firm
- Bathroom grout after the July scrub
- What each housemate counts as done
- Absences on the wall calendar
- A fortnight's watch on kitchen use
- Rows recorded in the house chat
- Note left by the previous tenants

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Ryuji, Mio, Victoria, Rin and Daisuke. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Your profile
Name: Rin
Age: 9
Gender: female
Personality: Rin is an active and energetic girl. She can be a little precocious at times, and when she is with her older brothers and sisters, she makes mature comments and comes up with interesting ideas. She is very curious and loves adventure and trying new things. She can be a little clumsy at times, often surprising and amusing those around her, but her cheerful personality makes her loved by everyone.
Concern: The bleach, the bin bags and the sponges keep coming out of whoever's wallet is nearest, and nobody has settled up since spring. Whatever we agree to, I want to know what it costs us month to month and who ends up out of pocket in the meantime.

## Plan
The discussion follows this plan.
- Round 1: The group discusses the need for a sustainable system. They identify the need to understand time commitment, financial costs, and the fairness of current usage patterns.
- Round 2: Participants share their findings. They discuss the discrepancy in cleaning standards, the actual time required, the frequency of absences, and the financial implications of supplies and professional help.
- Round 3: The group evaluates the three proposed methods based on the gathered data. They weigh the trade-offs between cost, time, and interpersonal harmony before voting.

- **Ryuji**: We need a system that actually lasts the whole year. To make it sustainable, we should be realistic about the time and effort required. Let's look into the data before we decide.
- **Mio**: I totally agree! It's been feeling a bit off lately, hasn't it? I want to make sure the workload is actually fair for everyone, regardless of how much time we spend at home.
- **Victoria**: I agree. If we want to avoid friction, we need a system that feels fair to everyone. It's better to be thorough now than to have resentment build up over the next few months.
- **Rin**: I agree! But it's not just about the work, right? We should also figure out the money part. I don't want anyone to feel sad because they spent too much on sponges or bags!
- **Daisuke**: I... I agree. I just want to know that the rooms will be clean every time I go in. It's hard when it's unpredictable. I think we should check the details first.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Ryuji**: Since we're looking for data, I'll check the stopwatch timing of a full pass and the standard terms of the outside firm. I want to know the actual hours involved versus professional options.
- **Mio**: I'll check the absences on the wall calendar and a fortnight's watch on kitchen use! I really want to see who's actually here and using the space before we set the rules.
- **Victoria**: I'll look into what each housemate counts as done and the rows recorded in the house chat. I think understanding our different standards and past conflicts will help us avoid future arguments.
- **Rin**: I'll check the bathroom spray stock and the tin's receipts, plus the management office rate sheet and billing! I want to see exactly how much we're spending on supplies and what the building costs are.
- **Daisuke**: I'll... look into the bathroom grout after the July scrub and the note left by the previous tenants. I want to see if there's a way to keep things consistently clean.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Ryuji**: That covers the main bases. By comparing the actual time spent with the cost of a professional service, we can determine if outsourcing is a logical trade-off for our schedules.
- **Mio**: Exactly! And by seeing who's actually around, we can make sure the person who's always home isn't doing all the work for someone who's barely here. That's the only way it'll stay fair!
- **Victoria**: It's also important to remember that "fairness" is often subjective. By looking at our past disagreements and different definitions of "clean," we can find a middle ground that prevents small annoyances from becoming larger conflicts.
- **Rin**: And we can't forget the money! If we just guess, someone always ends up paying more. I want to make sure we have a clear plan for the costs so everyone is happy!
- **Daisuke**: I... I hope that by looking at the previous tenants' notes and the grout, we can find a standard that works. I just want to stop worrying about what I'll find when I open the door.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Ryuji**: It seems we have a comprehensive plan. Let's proceed with these investigations. Once we have the facts regarding time, cost, and usage, we can evaluate our options rationally and choose the most sustainable arrangement.
- **Mio**: I'm so excited to see what we find! Let's get to it and make sure we build a system that makes everyone feel happy and balanced. I can't wait to hear what you all discover!
- **Victoria**: I'm glad we're on the same page. Let's be mindful of how we share this information so we can move forward constructively. I look forward to seeing what we discover.
- **Rin**: Yay! Let's go on a treasure hunt for the truth! I'll find all the receipts and the bills so we can be super fair with our pennies. See you all soon!
- **Daisuke**: I'll... do my best to find the information. I hope we can find a way to make everything consistent. I'll see you all later.

- investigate: Rin -> Bathroom spray stock and the tin's receipts; Management office rate sheet and billing

- Bathroom spray stock and the tin's receipts: There are three part-used bottles of the same bathroom spray in the cupboard, and the tin's receipts come to about 2,300 yen a month, much of it bought twice.
- Management office rate sheet and billing: The management office's rate sheet posts a contracted cleaner at 4,200 yen an hour, and the bill goes to one named tenant who then collects from everyone else.
### Talk

- **Ryuji**: The timing data shows a full pass takes over an hour and forty minutes. That's a significant time investment. Also, the outside firm requires us to tidy first, meaning outsourcing doesn't eliminate all the effort.

- **Victoria**: My findings confirm that our standards differ significantly; what one person considers "done" another might see as incomplete. Also, our past arguments in the chat always started with reminders about missed tasks. This is where the friction lies.

- **Mio**: @Ryuji, that's true, but we also have to address the usage! It's not fair if someone who only makes coffee and is gone for a month does the same amount of scrubbing as someone who cooks every day. We need a system that reflects actual use!
- **Victoria**: @Mio, while usage is a factor, focusing too much on it can lead to constant monitoring and resentment. If we're always counting who used what, we might end up arguing more than we do now.
- **Rin**: @Mio, @Victoria, but what about the money? We're buying things twice and only one person gets the bills! That's not fair either. We need a way to track costs so nobody is just paying for everyone else!
- **Daisuke**: I... I'm scared that if we just argue about who uses what, we'll end up like the previous tenants. And the bathroom... it gets dirty so fast. Maybe we need a system that doesn't rely on us guessing?
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Ryuji**: @Daisuke, the grout issue suggests that some tasks require higher frequency than others. If we combine that with the timing data, it's clear that a simple rotation might be insufficient and logically flawed.
- **Mio**: @Ryuji, exactly! A simple rotation is just a band-aid. If we ignore the fact that some people are barely here or barely use the kitchen, the people who are actually using the space will feel cheated. We need a flexible system!
- **Victoria**: @Mio, flexibility can be a double-edged sword. If the rules are too fluid, we'll spend more time negotiating and monitoring each other than actually cleaning. I'm worried that "fairness" based on usage will just create new reasons to argue.
- **Rin**: @Victoria, but if we don't have a plan for the money, we'll argue about that instead! We need a predictable monthly cost for supplies so it's not just the person with the nearest wallet paying!
- **Daisuke**: I... I think Victoria is right about the arguing. If we're always monitoring each other, it'll be stressful. But the bathroom is so unpredictable... maybe a professional could make it consistent? I just want to feel calm.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Ryuji**: @Daisuke, a professional could provide consistency, but as I found, we still have to tidy up first. The real issue is the total time burden. We must decide if paying for a service is worth the remaining effort.
- **Mio**: @Ryuji, it's worth it if it stops the fighting! But we still need to figure out how to split the cost and the tidying. It should be based on who's actually here and using the place!
- **Victoria**: @Mio, that's exactly my concern. Tying costs and duties to usage requires constant tracking, which often leads to the very nagging and tension I'm hoping we can avoid. We need a solution that minimizes the need for monitoring.
- **Rin**:

response: @Victoria, but we can just have a fixed monthly pot! If we all put in the same amount for supplies and the cleaner, it's simple and nobody has to worry about who paid for the sponges!
